full_judgment:
2. The appellant which was formerly Dhamai Tea Company Limited instituted Title Suit No. 76 of 1958 in the 2nd court of Munif, at Moulvi Bazar, Sylhet against one Arjun Kurmi, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1-3 and against the erstwhile Province of East Pakistan. The plaintiff-appellant prayed for declaration of title and khas possession of agricultural land measuring 10 bighas 7 kathas and 9 chataks which were given to Arjun Kurmi by the appellant on a licence renewable from year to year and as long as Arjun Kurmi was in its service. The licence fee was Tk. 1.00 per bighas per year, Arjun Kurmi who was a labourer of the Tea Estate was supposed to occupy the land as a licencee during the continuance of his service. As Arjun Kurmi was dismissed from service in July, 1958 be had no right to enjoy the land. 

 3. The suit was contested by Arjun Kurmi who asserted that the suit land was leased out to him by the then Manager of the appellant and he had been in possession of the land for 25/26 years as a tenant. He was, therefore, liable to be evicted. The Province of East Pakistan appeared in the suit but did neither file any written statement nor contest the suit. 

 5. Being aggrieved, by the judgment in Second Appeal No. 27 of 1966 the appellant moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the appellant gave a lease of the suit land to the respondents' predecessor, Arjun Kurmi, instead of a licence to stay on the suit Lund as long as he would be in the service of the Tea Estate. 

 "The difference between a tenancy and a licence is, therefore, that in a tenancy an interest passes in the land, whereas in a licence it does not. In distinguishing between them a crucial test has sometimes been supposed to be whether the occapier has exclusive possession or not. It he wall let into exclusive possession he was said to be a tenant, albeit only a tenant at will....................whereas if he had not exclusive possession he was only a licensee. ...... This test has however often given rise to misgivings because it may not correspond to realities.................The test of exclusive possession is by no means decisive." 

 16. It, however, appears that though the learned Judge of the High Court Division noted the principle laid down in these cases, be, after referring to two other case, namely. Addiscombe Garden Estates, Ltd, Vs. Crabee (1957) 2 All E.R. 563 and Finbow vs. Air Ministry, (1963) 2 All E.R. 647" concluded that since exclusive possession was held to be a consideration of first importance in these cases, in deciding whether a tenancy has been created or a mere licence has been granted, the respondents' exclusive possession strongly pointed in favour of tenancy. A fact of exclusive possession was established, according to him by the payment of rent by the respondents' predecessor to the appellant and also by the absence of exercise of any act of ownership by the appellant over the suit land during the 25 years. To my mind, the application of the principle of exclusive possession, as being of prime importance in determining whether there has been a tenancy or licence, to the facts of the instant case is misconceived. A Tea company requires workers for the purpose of plantation. It is all but natural that for ensuring the continuity of service by such workers and also efficiency they should be provided with certain amenities in addition to their salary. The appellant which is a tea company, therefore, offered the vacant lands inside the Tea Estate to the respondents' predecessor to stay on payment of Tk. 1/- per year as long as he would be in the appellant's service. This can by no means be construed as creating a tenancy in his favour. Salaries are distinct from amenities. The former is given for the service to be rendered the latter is allowed for ensuring efficiency of the service rendered by an employee. Amenities granted to an employee have to be exclusive. Any interference with such amenities would lead to harassment. If, therefore, the appellant did not interfere with the possession of the respondents' predecessor over 25 years, that merely shows that he was allowed to enjoy the amenities unhampered. This does not go to show that the appellant created a tenancy in his favour by not interfering with it. 

 17. As regards the contention that the suit lands being tenanted lands were acquired by the Government, it appears that no evidence has been given to show that the suit land falls outside the Tea Estate. Since the suit land falls within the Tea Estate and not outside, it comes within the exception mentioned in section 20, clause (5) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which provides "nothing in sub-sections (1), (2)and (3) of this section shall apply to any land held for the purpose of cultivation and manufacture of Tea Estate". In view or the exemption provided in the aforesaid provisions, the suit land having fallen within the appellant's Tea Estate cannot be said to come within the operation of the Sylhet Tenancy Act of 1930. Clause (V) of section I of this Act extends the Act to the district of Sylhet except "lands used for special cultivation or for purposes ancillary thereto so long as such use continues'. The provision in Explanation to clause (V) provides that "the words purposes ancillary thereto shall include the letting out of portion of such land for the maintenance of the coolies working on such cultivation". It was never the respondents' case that the suit land did not fall within the appellant's Tea Estate.
